issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s possession of land as khudkasht or sir is possession in law for the other co-sharers unless ouster is pleaded and established.
material_facts: A decree had recognized the claimant’s right as a co-sharer in the land.
Other co-sharers were found to be in exclusive actual possession of the disputed plots.
The finding was that the other co-sharers had not pleaded ouster.
issues.conclusion: The other co-sharers’ possession also counted as the claimant’s constructive possession, so the claimant could rely on the possession limb of section 18(1)(a).
issues.legal_principle: Section 18(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, includes constructive as well as actual possession. Under the general rule of co-sharer possession, one co-sharer possesses on behalf of all unless ouster is pleaded and established. Khudkasht is defined by section 3(9) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939, as land other than sir cultivated by a landlord, under-proprietor, or permanent tenure-holder, personally or through servants or hired labour. The Court found no indication in either Act that bhumidhari rights were excluded for co-sharers who were not themselves cultivating the land.

rule.if: land_reform_settlement_claim and coownership_right_recognized and another_coshare_in_possession and ouster_not_pleaded_or_established and land_is_sir_or_khudkasht

predicates.land_reform_settlement_claim: The claimant seeks recognition of land rights under a land-reform settlement scheme.
predicates.coownership_right_recognized: A legally recognized right establishes the claimant as a co-sharer in the land.
predicates.another_coshare_in_possession: Another co-sharer possesses the land, whether by actual occupation or cultivation.
predicates.ouster_not_pleaded_or_established: No other co-sharer has pleaded and established that the claimant was excluded from the shared possession.
predicates.land_is_sir_or_khudkasht: The land is of a kind whose possession can qualify for the settlement right at issue.

issues.definition: When a land-reform settlement claim concerns qualifying land jointly owned with a co-sharer in possession and no ouster is pleaded and established, the claimant is treated as being in constructive possession.

issues.legal_issue: For land qualifying as sir or khudkasht, being held or deemed to be held does not require the claimant’s own actual cultivation or physical possession.
material_facts: A prior decree had declared the claimant’s right and title as a co-sharer in the land.
Other co-sharers were found to be in actual possession, but the claimant’s title had not been defeated by an established ouster.
issues.conclusion: Even if the claimant was not in actual possession, the land could be treated as held or deemed to be held by the claimant because the claimant had a recognized right and title.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 18(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, settlement rights may arise where land is in an intermediary’s possession, held by the intermediary, or deemed to be held by the intermediary as sir or khudkasht. Following Budhan Singh v. Nabi Bux, the Court construed “held” as “lawfully held,” meaning held by legal title; it rejected the interpretation in Rama Kant Singh v. Deputy Director of Consolidation that undue emphasis on the individual co-proprietor’s cultivatory possession. The statutory alternatives permit a claim based on holding or deemed holding even where actual possession is absent.

predicates.land_reform_settlement_claim: The claimant seeks recognition of land rights under a land-reform settlement scheme.
predicates.claimant_has_recognized_lawful_title: A legally recognized right or title establishes the claimant’s lawful interest in the land.
predicates.land_is_sir_or_khudkasht: The land is of a kind whose holding can qualify for the settlement right at issue.

issues.definition: A claimant with recognized lawful title to qualifying land may be treated as holding or deemed to be holding it.

issues.legal_issue: A party need not appeal an interlocutory order calling for a factual finding before challenging the final decision based on that finding.
material_facts: During a second appeal, the High Court made an intermediate order calling for a finding about possession.
The claimant did not appeal that intermediate order and challenged the High Court’s final decision after it accepted the finding.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was justified in waiting for the High Court’s final decision and was not barred from challenging it for failing to appeal the intermediate order.
issues.legal_principle: An order calling for a finding at an intermediary stage is not a final decision that the party must separately appeal before challenging the eventual judgment; the Court applied this principle to the procedural history of the appeal.

predicates.appeal_against_final_decision: A party appeals from the court’s final decision.
predicates.challenged_order_was_interlocutory: The earlier order was made at an intermediate stage and called for a factual finding rather than finally deciding the dispute.
predicates.final_decision_relied_on_later_finding: The court’s final decision relied on the finding obtained under the intermediate order.

issues.definition: When a final decision relies on a finding sought by an interlocutory order, a party appealing the final decision may challenge it without first appealing that order.
